To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the erythrocytes contain a protein- and ATP-dependent transporter that moves phospholipid molecules from the outer to inner monolayer of the membrane.

the ATP-dependent flippase in the erythroocyte membrane has broader specificity for lipid substrates than previously thought, and that the transport of phosphatidyserine analogs is not the only function of the aminophosphatidyl flippase.

the ATP-dependent transbilayer movement (flipping) of phospholipid molecules in the erythroocyte membrane is restricted to phospholipids with negatively-charged head groups, such as phosphatidylcholines, and that this flipping is inhibited by the ATPase inhibitor, vanadate, and the sulfhydryl reagent, N-ethylmaleamide.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the transmembrane lipid movement in human erythroocytes.
the study of the transbilayer distribution of phospholipid species and their transbilayer movement in human red cell membranes.
the transbilayer movement and distribution of lipids in biological membranes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the flippases of the red cell plasma membrane are capable of translocating a variety of phospholipid molecules from the outer leaflet to the inner leaflet.
the flippases are able to transport PS and PE, but not other lipids.
the flippases in erythrocytes and other cell types are capable of transporting a variety of phospholipid substrates.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the erythrocytes aminophosphlipid flippase is a protein- and ATP-dependent translocase that catalyzes the transport of phosphatidyserine (PS), phosphatidyletanolamine (PE), and other lipids from the outer to inner monolayer, while the other phospholipid translocators (flip-flops) move lipids only by passive diffusion.
the flippases are more specific than previously thought.
the flippases have broad specificity for substrates.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the flippases are not specific for PS or PE, but rather for negatively charged phospholipids.
there is more than one protein involved in lipid transport in the erythrocell membrane.
there is more to phospholipid asymmetry in the plasma membrane than the aminophosphlipid flippase.
